title: Buffett's 1980 letter: retained earnings, inflation as a hidden tax, and GEICO
summary: Buffett argues that the economic value of retained earnings depends on how they are used, not on accounting credit or ownership percentage. He explains why inflation turns ordinary corporate returns into negative real returns for owners, why GEICO is a rare franchise with a skilled manager, and why insurers should be wary of bond-driven price cutting.

principles.text: Retained earnings are worth what they earn when put to use, regardless of whether you own 1% or 100% or get accounting credit.
principles.quote: The value to Berkshire Hathaway of retained earnings is not determined by whether we own 100%, 50%, 20% or 1% of the businesses in which they reside. Rather, the value of those retained earnings is determined by the use to which they are put

principles.text: Prefer unrecorded earnings reinvested well by a good management over credited earnings reinvested poorly, even by yourself.
principles.quote: we would rather have earnings for which we did not get accounting credit put to good use in a 10%-owned company by a management we did not personally hire, than have earnings for which we did get credit put into projects of more dubious potential by another management - even if we are that management.

principles.text: Buybacks are the best use of capital when a fine business trades far below intrinsic value; markets often offer cheaper earning power than takeovers.
principles.quote: if a fine business is selling in the market place for far less than intrinsic value, what more certain or more profitable utilization of capital can there be than significant enlargement of the interests of all owners at that bargain price?

principles.text: Only gains in purchasing power are real earnings; inflation is a tax on capital that can make a decent return negative.
principles.quote: For only gains in purchasing power represent real earnings on investment.

principles.text: Turnarounds rarely work: when brilliant management meets a business with poor economics, the business's reputation usually survives intact.
principles.quote: with few exceptions, when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for poor fundamental economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact.

principles.text: The best investments pair a hard-to-duplicate business advantage with management skilled in both operations and capital allocation.
principles.quote: GEICO represents the best of all investment worlds - the coupling of a very important and very hard to duplicate business advantage with an extraordinary management whose skills in operations are matched by skills in capital allocation.
